posts.copy:
Last week, I posted a PMP scenario:

A sponsor wants to skip a planned stakeholder review to hit a date. The team can meet the date, but a high-impact dependency may be affected. What do you do first?

Three people answered. All three chose the same thing — assess the dependency impact with the relevant stakeholders — and all three were right.

Bryan Koh gave the reason rather than just the letter: the question asks what you do FIRST. You ASSESS, before you act.

Here's the part worth noting:

"Assess first" is correct here, but it isn't a rule. It's a response to one word in the stem: "may." A high-impact dependency MAY be affected. That's unresolved uncertainty, and you can't accept it, escalate it, or document your way out of not knowing.

Change that one word and the answer changes with it.

If the stem said the dependency WILL slip go-live by three weeks, the uncertainty is already resolved. Assessing again is stalling. Now the real choice is between escalating and replanning — and "assess" becomes the wrong answer.

That's what the updated exam is actually testing: act at the level of information the scenario gives you.

Candidates who memorize "always assess first" pass the easy version of this question and miss the hard one, because the hard version already did the assessing for them.

The tell is in the verb. "May be affected" means go find out. "Will be affected" means ... decide.

#PMP #ProjectManagement

Quick Security+ scenario.

A junior admin emails you: "Production database server's been compromised. I'm isolating it from the network now — should I also shut it down?"

The instinct answer is yes. Pull the plug, contain the threat.

Most Sec+ prep tools mark "shut down" as correct because it sounds like containment.

The exam doesn't.

CompTIA writes this scenario to test whether you understand that shutting down a live system destroys volatile memory — running processes, network connections, decryption keys — which is exactly what an incident responder needs to capture first. Availability is one leg of the CIA triad, but so is the integrity of forensic evidence.

The right answer under exam reasoning: isolate, image, then power off. Order matters.

posts.priorCopy:
Business Environment moved from 8% of the PMP to 26% on July 9, 2026.

Compliance sits inside that domain. Those scenarios now carry roughly three times the weight.

Try one. A stakeholder tells you a regulatory requirement was missed. Release is two weeks out.

You can raise a change request. You can escalate to the sponsor. You can rework the schedule with your team. You can confirm the requirement with the compliance owner.

Four options, and a working PM has done all four on a real Tuesday.

Most experienced PMs reach for the change request. It is documented, it is defensible, and on the job it is the right call.

On the exam, second.

A change request assumes you already know what is changing. Read the stem again. Someone told you a requirement was missed. Nothing in it establishes that the requirement applies, what it costs, or who owns the decision.

Confirming with the compliance owner tests whether the gap is real and puts the call with the person accountable for it.

Run the same rule on a different question. Two team members disagree on an approach. Decide for them. Escalate to the sponsor. Bring them together to work the problem.

Deciding and escalating both end the conversation. Nothing in the stem says it has to end. Collaborate keeps both people in it, and it is the only option that produces a solution both of them own.

Read the stem for what has actually been established. Then pick the option that works at that line.

PMI grouped PMP situational questions into case sets on July 9. Three to five questions per project scenario.

That changes the math on a wrong read.

Miss the frame on a standalone question and it costs you one question. Miss it on question 1 of a case set and questions 2 through 5 inherit it. Read the project as predictive when it's actually hybrid, and you answer all five from inside that mistake.

One bad read. Five wrong answers.

The trap underneath is subtler. By question 3 you've already committed to a reading, and staying consistent with it feels like discipline. It isn't. If a later question in a set doesn't sit right, that's information about your frame, not just about that question.

Three of the four options are usually defensible anyway. Only one matches how PMI wants you to think.

I wrote up the lens I use to pick it, five worked scenarios, and the five traps — including the case-set one. Free — link in the first comment.
